transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-03-05
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~62 min
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Elliot Ruiz (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (EdenFlow), Liam O'Reilly (EdenFlow), Sara Montenegro (EdenFlow)

Summary:
Quick partner intro between Redwood and EdenFlow HPC to explore an onramp integration for EdenFlow's SaaS HPC offering. Primary themes: connectivity (VPC/peering), model serving performance on EdenFlow GPUs, quantization & model variants, billing/integrations for reseller partner. Agreed to follow up with technical deep dive focused on network and perf tests.

Topics covered:
- Partner model (reseller vs co-hosted) and contract framing
- Private control plane vs shared control plane tradeoffs
- Workload profiles (batching, latency SLOs, long-context LLMs)
- Security: SOC2, KMS, audit logs, data residency
- Pilot design and success criteria

Action items (also in metadata): see action_items field.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Maya, AE on the partnerships team at Redwood, with Elliot our solutions engineer.
[00:12] Elliot Ruiz: Hi all, quick wave. Excited to learn about EdenFlow and see where we can plug in.
[00:18] Priya Singh: Hi Maya, Elliot. Thanks for setting this up. I'm Priya, I run infra. Couple of high level context points from our side—EdenFlow runs a multitenant SaaS HPC cluster, we sell GPU time as a service, typical customers are genomics and inference-heavy ML teams.
[00:34] Liam O'Reilly: And I'm Liam, CTO. We're exploring ways to offer an LLM inference onramp to our customers, but we don't want to become a model maintainer. We're interested in routing + billing and possibly reselling Redwood's hosted inference.
[00:48] Sara Montenegro: Hey, Sara here — platform eng. I manage the on-prem and VPC connectors and will be hands on if we move forward.
[00:56] Maya Chen: Awesome, thanks. Quick question on workloads — are you expecting mostly short-chat style calls or long-context user chat, batch scoring, embeddings?
[01:07] Priya Singh: Mix, but leaning toward longer context for a subset — customers want 8k-32k token sequences for document understanding; we also see batch embedding workloads overnight.
[01:18] Elliot Ruiz: Got it. That suggests tradeoffs for memory/KV cache and batching. For longer contexts you'll want models with attention optimizations and we can recommend quant profiles. Also routing policies matter — we can support routing by latency vs cost so you can offer tiers.
[01:34] Liam O'Reilly: Can you explain the difference between Redwood's Dedicated offering vs a private control plane? We want to know what the integration surface would be.
[01:42] Maya Chen: Sure. Hosted Redwood API is a multi-tenant hosted service — low friction for your customers but you'd be reselling managed capacity. Dedicated means reserved GPU pools for a partner or customer with isolation and SLA. Private deployment is where you run Redwood's control plane in your VPC or on-prem — that gives you full data residency and integration with your KMS/HSM.
[02:00] Speaker 3: (murmur)
[02:05] Priya Singh: For EdenFlow, data residency and audit logs are important for our regulated customers; if we resell a hosted model we need to see SOC2 and audit capabilities.
[02:14] Maya Chen: Understood — we have SOC2 docs and we can share SOC2 + ISO artifacts through our partner portal. We also support KMS integrations for key management and detailed audit logs per request.
[02:25] Sara Montenegro: Walk me through connectivity — if we do a private control plane, do you require peering? VPN? What's the latency overhead?
[02:33] Elliot Ruiz: For Private, typically a VPC peering or private link to the control plane and then worker nodes can be in your VPC. Latency is essentially your network latency plus a tiny orchestration hop. For Dedicated you could also colocate workloads in your region — peering recommended for best security. If you want zero egress for tokens, running the private control plane on-prem is the path.
[02:54] Liam O'Reilly: What about the serving runtime — is it flexible with kernels and quantization? We use mixed-precision and have both A100 and H100 fleets.
[03:04] Elliot Ruiz: Yes, our runtime picks kernels based on model arch and hardware. We have paths for quantized int8/4 as well as float fp16. For H100 we use a different optimized kernel set; we can profile and recommend quantization profiles per model. But note, extreme quant can impact quality — we tie recommendations with Redwood Optimize to guard regressions.
[03:23] Priya Singh: Are there known perf numbers for 8k and 32k token context? We need rough guesstimates for pricing.
[03:30] Elliot Ruiz: I can run a perf matrix. Rough ballpark: for an 8k context on an A100 optimized kernel, throughput X and p50 latency ~200-400ms per chunk depending on batch. For 32k it scales nonlinearly. I'll put concrete numbers in a follow-up spreadsheet.
[03:48] Maya Chen: We'll include an initial benchmark table. Also we usually recommend prefix/KV caching for long context applications to reduce token cost.
[03:56] Sara Montenegro: We do have customers that stream long documents and interrupted sessions; caching could be huge for cost. How does Redwood handle fallback if capacity spikes?
[04:07] Elliot Ruiz: We have smart routing and can fall back to cheaper/compatible model variants or different regions. For partners we can configure routing policies so critical customers hit Dedicated pools first and others use burst capacity.
[04:19] Liam O'Reilly: On billing — we need integration into our billing system if we resell. Can we get usage logs by tenant and token-level breakdown?
[04:28] Maya Chen: Yes, Redwood Console exposes token-level cost and latency breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and exportable billing reports. For reseller partners we support partner-facing billing APIs and usage CSVs.
[04:39] Priya Singh: Security review — we will want SAML SSO for the control plane, RBAC, and audit logs. Any blockers?
[04:47] Maya Chen: SAML SSO is supported, RBAC is fine, and we provide audit logs incl. request/response metadata retention options. For compliance we can do a joint security questionnaire; I'll send our security deck.
[04:58] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[05:05] Sara Montenegro: What about model updates and rollouts? If our customers pin a model version, can Redwood handle canary rollouts across partner Dedicated pools?
[05:14] Elliot Ruiz: Yes — rollouts, canary, A/B tests, automatic fallbacks are part of our deployment abstraction. You can pin versions per-tenant.
[05:22] Liam O'Reilly: For the pilot, we'd probably want an MVP where we integrate routing and billing and run a tiny pilot with 3 customers. What success metrics should we track?
[05:30] Maya Chen: Typical pilot metrics: per-request p50/p95 latency, cost per 1k tokens, model output quality (we can tie evaluation prompts), error rates, and integration friction (time to onboard single tenant).
[05:41] Priya Singh: On the tech side, Sara will send network diagrams. We'll want a repo of sample configs for your control plane and a small infra guide.
[05:50] Elliot Ruiz: I'll prepare a partner runbook and sample terraform snippets for peering and worker node setup.
[05:56] Speaker 2: (crosstalk)
[06:02] Priya Singh: A few quick risks from our side — we have strict egress controls for some customers and some air-gapped tenants. Can Redwood run in an air-gapped environment?
[06:11] Maya Chen: Yes, we have an on-prem package for air-gapped deployments that includes a private control plane and offline distro of the runtime. That usually requires an enterprise agreement and a bit of setup.
[06:22] Liam O'Reilly: Competition — we've spoken with Lambda and CoreWeave about reseller programs. How do you typically differentiate from them in partner talks?
[06:30] Maya Chen: We emphasize production-first ops — observability, deterministic unit economics controls like intelligent batching/caching, and seamless parity across hosted/dedicated/private. Also our model catalog and Optimize toolkit make it easier to reduce costs without blind quality hits.
[06:46] Elliot Ruiz: And our runtime's kernel selection and KV caching is often a technical differentiator for long-context workloads.
[06:52] Sara Montenegro: I have a small technical question — for KV cache persistence across restarts, what's the recommended approach?
[06:59] Elliot Ruiz: Short answer: KV cache is in-memory for low latency but we support snapshotting for warm starts and prefix caching for common prompts. For long-lived sessions we recommend a hybrid approach — store prefixes in your own store and let Redwood rehydrate caches. I'll add docs.
[07:16] Priya Singh: Ok let's talk timeline. If we decide to pilot, earliest we can start is late March. Our Q2 goal is to have a reseller offering live, so timeline is tight.
[07:27] Maya Chen: That timeline is reasonable. Action items: we'll send partner deck and SOC2, Elliot runs perf estimates, Sara sends network docs, and we schedule a technical deep dive next week focused on quantization and kernel profiling.
[07:42] Liam O'Reilly: Sounds good. One more question — can Redwood support multiple hardware types within the same routing policy? E.g., H100 for latency-sensitive customers, A100 for cost-sensitive?
[07:51] Elliot Ruiz: Yes, routing policies can be hardware-aware. You can set region + hardware + model variant priorities.
[07:59] Priya Singh: Great. That flexibility is key for our customers.
[08:04] Maya Chen: We'll follow up with links: partner deck, security pack, and a proposed pilot scope doc. I'll put tentative dates for the deep dive in the calendar.
[08:15] Sara Montenegro: Thanks everyone.
[08:18] Liam O'Reilly: Thanks, talk soon.
[08:20] Maya Chen: Thanks all — we'll circulate notes and next steps. Bye.

Notes on transcript quality and quirks: automated transcription had trouble with a few proper nouns (EdenFlow sometimes transcribed as 'Eden' or 'Edenflowe'), 'KV cache' occasionally became 'K V cash' in the raw text. Some timestamps approximate speaker switches.
